title: Foundation English for University Studies
requirements: Not for students who have taken ELTU1002
description: This course aims to lay the comprehensive English language foundation needed for university studies by engaging students in multi-modal learning activities. In particular, students are guided to plan and complete an argumentative problem-solution essay and deliver corresponding presentations using research, writing and speaking skills acquired in the course. Learning topics include: identifying features of academic writing, distinguishing and presenting arguments, conducting academic research, documenting sources, paraphrasing and summarising, structuring presentations, and enhancing verbal and non-verbal delivery skills. Course-tied workshops will be provided in support of students’ learning. This course is compulsory for first-year students, except for those who have attained HKDSE English level 5 or above or its equivalence.

description: This course is designed to help students with a good level of English proficiency to learn essential academic English skills for university studies. In particular, the course will focus on the development of academic essays based on library and Internet research. Course content includes topic, purpose and audience analyses, evaluating digital source materials and research methods, summarizing, paraphrasing and synthesizing skills, proper documentation of sources, presentation practice, peer reviews and self-access online learning. Course-tied workshops will be provided in support of students’ learning. title: Critical Thinking in English Language Communication

description: This course is designed for Year 1 students with an advanced level of English language proficiency (HKDSE level 5* or above or its equivalence). The aim of this course is to facilitate their development of analytical and critical reasoning skills through the study of inductive reasoning. In particular, this course will focus on the acquisition of skills necessary for the analysis and evaluation of inductive arguments in the English language. Topics that will be included in the course include: identifying assumptions, standardizing and diagramming arguments in the English language, fallacies of irrelevance, inductive reasoning, and inductive fallacies.Samples of argumentation will be taken from both text-based sources (e.g. op-eds, articles, essays, etc.) and multimedia sources (e.g. movie clips, video recordings, advertisements, etc.) composed in the English language, to enhance students’ awareness of and appreciation for argumentation techniques that are variously employed in both academic and non-academic settings.As this is a Level 1 course requiring frequent intensive engagements with source materials, the importance of academic integrity and effective source-use skills will also be discussed.Advisory: this course assumes the attainment of an advanced level of English language proficiency, as demonstrated by a grade of HKDSE level 5* or above or its equivalence.

title: Speaking and Presenting like TED
requirements: Pre-requisite(s): ELTU1001 or ELTU1002 or exemption from these courses
description: The course aims to inspire students to speak and present more like TED. The course adopts a learning-by-doing approach: students are expected to come to class prepared to share their critical analyses of TED talks and present ideas in their respective academic discipline. Students will teach each other by: a) analyzing the content, delivery, language, design and use of visuals in TED talks; b) presenting their critical analyses in class; c) applying the results of the analyses in mini-presentations; d) creating strategies to deal with discipline-specific norms; and e) evaluating and giving feedback to each other.Advisory: For students with above-average listening and speaking proficiency in English, e.g., DSE 4 or above.

title: English Through Literary Analysis
requirements: Prerequisite: ELTU1001 or ELTU1002 or exemption from these courses
description: In this course, students of the Faculty of Arts will read different texts such as short stories, novellas and parts of novels and explore other forms of media (such as visual art, film and television). These serve as means for students to learn about some well-established critical approaches in literary theory and engage actively in discussion regarding the content and ideas in the texts, as well as the writing strategies used by the authors. These concepts in literature are universal throughout the Humanities and it is hoped that through this course, students will develop their critical thinking skills via textual analyses and that these skills can be transferred to their own disciplines. The texts and film adaptations cover different genres, cultural backgrounds and eras with topics that will focus on social change. These texts and adaptations will be used to highlight different critical literary approaches used in analyses of literature and film. Students are expected to apply these ‘lenses’ to their own writing and to critically evaluate their work and the work of their classmates. Participation in class discussions of the assigned readings is crucial – which means reading or viewing the texts in preparation for each class is essential.
outcome: By the end of this course students will be able to: Analyze a literary text using different critical theories; Compose an original, logical and well-reasoned academic paper in the form of a literary analysis essay; Deliver an analytical presentation/discussion based on their literary analysis essay; and Undertake in-depth analysis and evaluation/critique of their own written work and the work of their classmates.
syllabus: Learning topics include: Feminist Literary Theory Students learn how characters, especially the female characters, are portrayed and how the portrayal of female characters reinforces or undermines sexual stereotypes.   Marxist Literary Theory Students learn the role of class (social and economic standing) and ideology (main underlying principles) in literature as they reflect, promote, and sometimes challenge the prevailing social order. They will focus on how those in power seek to maintain that power, in part by justifying it through art and literature. They will also focus on the struggle that exists between the working class and the ruling (elite) class.   Postcolonial Literary Theory Students learn to read for an awareness of representation of non-Europeans as exotic or ‘Other’ in literature. They also learn to focus on language to see if the colonizer's language is permanently tainted, to write in it involves acquiescence in colonial structures. Other topics include observing the identity as doubled or unstable (identify with colonizer and colonized) in literature, and also learn to be aware of cross-cultural interactions within literary work.These topics are transferrable to various disciplines in the Faculty of Arts. These concepts are also universal in understanding the trends in humanities. Understanding them will help students develop their critical thinking and develop their use of the English language in critiquing, discussing and analyzing film and literature.

description: This course is designed for second-year students in the Faculty of Education to improve their powers of persuasion through spoken and written academic English. As such, the course emphasizes an understanding and application of the language of persuasion – or ethos, logos, and pathos – as well as discussion skills, academic presentation skills, questioning skills, and the development of persuasive writing based on research. title: English through Popular Art and Culture
requirements: Prerequisite: (ELTU1001 or ELTU1002 or exemption from these courses) and (ELTU2004 or ELTU2005 or ELTU2006 or ELTU2011 or ELTU2022 or ELTU2406 or ELTU2412 or exemption from these courses)
description: ELTU3010 English through Popular Art and Culture is a multidisciplinary, interest-oriented level-three course tailored for students from diverse academic backgrounds across the Faculty of Arts at CUHK. The course focuses on developing curation and narration—complementary spoken and written communication skills—to support students’ language development within and beyond their undergraduate studies. The course emphasises how curation and narration, essential language skills that play a pivotal role in everyday acts of meaning-making, can be applied to popular art and appreciation through a theme-based approach. Themes include, but are not limited to, identity and soul, truth and beauty, pain and trauma, love and hate, explored across disciplines within the settings of Popular Art and Culture. Each theme, delivered as a module, is taught through a variety of popular art forms, such as theatre and drama, television, film and anime, media, documentary, popular music, literature, and the fine arts. Lessons are structured around class activities designed to illustrate the principles of curation and narration using selected sources. Each week, students engage with a diverse range of materials, including readings, video excerpts, songs, and visual or digital art, all aligned with the lesson's theme.The course also aims to deepen students’ awareness of the humanities—how people understand, interpret, and communicate about the world and their place in it—through engagement with the module themes and class activities. In this course, curation extends beyond traditional gallery, exhibition, or museum contexts to include verbal presentations that involve the selection, organisation, and interpretation of subject matter within Popular Art and Culture. Narration refers to the written articulation, based on the verbal presentation, that structures and conveys meaning through analysis and storytelling. Upon completing the course, students will have acquired the ability to adapt and integrate these spoken and written communication strategies into their own areas of study and interest, enhancing their discipline-specific presentation and expression. They will develop not only linguistic competence but also creative confidence in expressing ideas across cultural and artistic contexts.Advisory: Year 3 students of the Faculty of Arts.

title: English for MBChB Programme: Medicine in the Humanities
requirements: Prerequisite: ELTU1001 or ELTU1002 or exemption from these courses
description: ELTU3017, Medical in the Humanities (also known as “Medical Humanities”), has been designed in close coordination with the Faculty of Medicine at CUHK. This course is multi-disciplinary and considers how doctors and health are presented through films, images, literature, poetry, and the media, and how students can prepare in a humanistic way to meet the challenges of a career as a physician. The topic list is broad, including the physician-patient relationship, narrative medicine and storytelling, intercultural communication, stereotyping in the health professions, ideas about death and dying (as they relate to spiritual beliefs and organ donation), the pitfalls and potential of integrated medicine, the management of medical information in the media and how the Internet impacts patients and doctors, amongst other topics. Particularly, the course is designed to develop students’ skills in close reading, attentive listening, critical thinking, impromptu speaking, analyzing videos and texts, and reflective writing. There will be one assigned reading and topic each week, and students should be prepared to present the text in class and/or engage in panel discussions about it.
outcome: By the end of this course, students will have further developed their skills in: Critical and close reading by analyzing texts in the field of Medical Humanities. Analyzing the language, expression and narrative of texts, films and images concerning the history and practice of medicine. Structuring and delivering short, impromptu presentations that emphasize professionalism, organization, and English-speaking skills. Attentive listening and critical thinking through the use of video materials, followed by tasks including reflecting and evaluating, summarizing, presenting, and writing responses.

title: Effective Data-Driven Communication in English for Academic and Professional Contexts
requirements:
Prerequisites:
ELTU1001 or 1002 or exemption from these courses AND
ELTU2004 or 2005 or 2006 or 2011 or 2013 or 2014 or 2016 or 2017 or 2018 or 2019 or 2020 or 2022 or 2023 or 2024 or 2026 or 2406 or 2412 or exemption from these courses
description: This course seeks to equip undergraduate students across various disciplines to develop persuasive data-driven spoken and written communication in English for academic and professional purposes. Students will learn how to describe, interpret and apply different data visualization and storytelling techniques to deliver quantitative information across physical and virtual contexts, in both academic and professional communicative settings. Emphasis will be placed on language precision, clarity in visual design, and adaptability of communication strategies to different audiences and communicative goals (e.g., informing, justifying, recommending, advocating).
outcome: By the end of this course, students will be able to: Demonstrate clarity, concision and coherence in data-driven communication that informs and persuades in both academic and professional contexts. Evaluate and select appropriate visualization types that effectively support key messages and persuasive goals for specific data sets in different communicative contexts, both physical and virtual. Critically evaluate visuals for clarity, accuracy, potential bias and persuasive effects. Develop clear data-driven narratives that communicate insights, support claims and justify recommendations. Adapt data-rich content and persuasive strategies for different communicative purposes (e.g., to inform, justify, recommend or advocate) and audiences. Develop rhetorical literacy in the context of AI-human collaborative writing.
syllabus: Learning topics include: Intentional design and persuasive communication of data in academic and professional contexts Audience awareness and purpose: informing, convincing and motivating action with data Writing data commentaries that interpret, evaluate and argue from quantitative evidence Effective data visualization and storytelling for persuasion in reports, posters and presentations Ethical data visualization and avoiding misleading or manipulative use of data

description: This course aims to help students become more effective and confident public speakers. Learning topics include vocal variation, diction, rhetoric, formality and delivery. title: Intercultural Communication Through English
requirements: Pre-requisites: ELTU1001 or ELTU1002 or exemption from these courses AND ELTU2004 or 2005 or 2006 or 2011 or 2013 or 2014 or 2016 or 2017 or 2018 or 2019 or 2020 or 2022 or 2023 or 2024 or 2026 or 2406 or 2412 or exemption from these courses
description: Developing intercultural competencies is a lifelong process. This course aims to enhance students’ intercultural communication skills in English, while fostering global citizenship. Throughout the course, students are guided to develop the attitudes, skills, and knowledge which can facilitate meaningful intercultural communication. Students will engage in tasks such as reading, watching videos, discussions, and the analysis of intercultural dialogues to help them to become more global-minded interculturally competent speakers of English.The main course objectives are to practice deep listening (i.e., listening for understanding), suspend snap judgments about cultural difference, and increase cultural awareness of self and others. In other words, the course aims to develop some of the core attributes that are expected of CUHK graduates i.e., intercultural understanding and sensitivity, and global-mindedness.
outcome: By the end of this course, students will be able to: demonstrate a critical understanding of what meaningful intercultural communication entails; demonstrate the ability to recognize and appreciate cultural and linguistic diversity; make reasoned verbal and non-verbal choices in intercultural encounters; produce coherent, insightful accounts of their intercultural experience in English; and reflect on and assess their L2/ cultural self-awareness and intercultural communication skills, and set realistic goals for further enhancement of their English language proficiency, intercultural competence, and global-mindedness.
syllabus: Learning topics include: Introduction to language and intercultural communication • understanding language and intercultural communication • identifying the attitudes, skills, and knowledge that facilitate intercultural communication Language and non-verbal communication • understanding, discussing, and analyzing the relationship between language, communication, culture, power and context • identifying different types and functions of nonverbal codes • discussing and explaining the influence of culture on non-verbal communication • practicing intercultural communication skills in English Language and identity in intercultural communication • identifying multiple characteristics of identity • describing the relationship between language, culture and identity • explaining the role of identity in intercultural communication • reflecting on one’s identity and how it affects one’s language use in context Language and intercultural relationships • discussing, identifying, and analyzing factors that affect intercultural relations in different contexts • explaining the potential impact of culture in conflict situations • discussing and presenting strategies for dealing effectively and appropriately with intercultural conflicts • practicing intercultural communication skills in English Global citizenship and intercultural competence • identifying the traits and characteristics of global citizens • describing ways to enhance one’s intercultural competence and intercultural/global citizenry • practicing intercultural communication skills in English

title: Postgraduate Presentation Skills
description: This course is designed for postgraduate students who want to upgrade their spoken English and presentation skills for academic purposes. Specifically, it focuses on developing effective communication skills for tutorials, proposals/protocols, seminars, conferences and oral defence. Students will be introduced to key concepts and strategies, such as audience-awareness, the power of summary, vocal advantage, and effective delivery of well-organized content materials using visual aids. Coursework consists of oral presentations and discussion of a wide variety of academic output.
outcome: By the end of the course, students should be able to:  1. develop an ability to plan and organize ideas logically in a formal setting; 2. develop an appreciation of the importance of English presentation skills; 3. build confidence step by step in presenting academic outputs in formal settings; 4. present the gist of a research study, thesis, or statement of purpose concisely; 5. speak with clarity (in lay language) on their chosen area of special interest and adequately answer questions from at the audience; 6. strike a balance between the audience, the speaker, and content; and 7. self-evaluate and give feedback to peers on various presentations.
syllabus: 1) Course Familiarization - Introduction to the course structure  - teaching topics - assessment structure - project requirements - resources  2) Principles and Practice - Skills and strategies in giving presentations  - reflecting on one’s speaking abilities (e.g. pre-course speaking ex.) - developing good habits of better speaking in English - clear articulation and pronunciation practice  3) Honesty in Academic Work - Quoting, paraphrasing, summarizing skills when using secondary resources  - Referencing and giving credit where it is due  4) Seminar Skills - Planning and leading a seminar  - addressing basic requirements of the seminar - answering basic seminar questions and objectives - chairing a seminar - leading and taking part in academic discussions  5) Giving Prepared Speeches - Preparing a formal speech  - Setting goals and objectives - Understanding the audience - Gathering details - Summarizing main ideas - Organizing and presenting them - Delivering the speech - Showing position, problem, possibilities and making a proposal - Developing greater confidence and skills in delivery  6) Giving impromptu speeches - Understanding and meeting basic requirements  - The challenge of thinking on your feet - Giving impromptu talk and not talking impromptu - Practicing and meeting expectations of the audience  7) Final Speech Project in Persuasion - Putting it all together and presenting your case  - Element of persuasion: appeals and logic, evidence / support - Structure of persuasion - Process of developing a persuasive writing strategy - Presenting the problem, method, solution, benefits, proposal

title: Grammar in Context
requirements: Not for students who have taken ELTU1106
description: This course aims to help students acquire conceptual understanding of English grammar with a specific focus on areas that are most problematic for university students. To enhance a conceptual understanding, the course encourages an inductive approach to grammar rules, using a variety of texts for illustration of grammatical features in use. Both spoken and written contexts will be used There will be various language activities, games and exercises to raise students’ awareness of the contextualized use of English grammar. Coursework includes grammar exercises, self-access language learning (SALL) assignments, a mid-term test, a grammar project and a final examination. Advisory: For students who have attained HKDSE English level 3 or 4 or its equivalence.

title: English Through Popular Culture
requirements: Prerequisite(s): ELTU1001 or ELTU1002 or exemption from these courses
description: This course aims to develop language skills and vocabulary through the analysis of stimuli from popular culture. Students will increase their ability to analyze such materials from a cultural and linguistic perspective, and to speak fluently and accurately about them. Additionally, students will develop an awareness of learning strategies for maximizing the potential of such materials in their own independent learning. Coursework includes analysis of songs, films and television shows and strategy development for using popular culture materials in academic and language learning. This 2-unit course is suitable for students from all faculties, and prerequisites are ELTU 1001 or ELTU 1002 or exemption from these courses.

title: English through the Visual Arts
requirements: Pre-requisite(s): ELTU1001 or ELTU1002 or exemption from these courses
description: This course is designed for students who have an interest in visual art and who would like to learn how to talk meaningfully about their personal interest. Along with developing the necessary language tools associated with art, students will be provided with many opportunities to describe, analyse and critique works of art. Coursework is made up of two components: the first component is provided by the teacher, and consists of the basic guidelines and materials necessary for developing this communication skill. The second consists of a teacher-approved programme of learning activities that is to be designed by the students themselves, either individually or in pairs. Advisory: Recommended for Year 2 students of the Faculty of Arts.

title: English Through Creative Writing
description: This course aims to strengthen English language skills by introducing students to Creative Writing. Learning topics include short stories, creative non-fiction, poetry and the revision process. Coursework consists of a Creative Writing portfolio, a short reflective essay and a public reading project. This 2-unit course is an elective for all undergraduate students (except ENGE and ELED students).

title: English Through Film
description: This is an integrated theme-based course designed for students who want to improve their English analytical and discussion skills. Specifically, it will focus on the analysis of linguistic, cultural and intellectual aspects of films. Coursework will include class discussions of assigned films (viewed outside of class), a series of short talks prepared by students on an aspect of film, a written essay and a group presentation. This course is particularly suitable for students who feel confident in their English-language abilities.
